# Ray Traversal and Integration Schemes

Also called: Ray Marching, Ray Casting Loop, Integration Methods

## Overview
Ray Traversal and Integration Schemes define how scalar voxel values are aggregated along a viewing ray to produce a final pixel intensity, ranging from simple statistical projections to physically-based [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) [S1, S2, S3, unofficial]. They solve the problem of mapping 3D volumetric data to 2D image space by determining which voxel properties (intensity, opacity, depth) contribute to the final pixel color [S2, unofficial]. Unlike [Ray Marching and Discretization](2788-ray-marching-and-discretization.md), which focuses on the spatial sampling of the ray, these schemes focus on the mathematical aggregation function applied to the sampled values [S2, unofficial]. They differ from [Monte Carlo Path Tracing for Volume Rendering](4980-monte-carlo-path-tracing-for-volume-rendering.md) by typically using deterministic, sequential accumulation rather than stochastic sampling [S4, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The core computational engine consists of four sequential stages applied to each ray [S5, S10, S37, unofficial]:

1.  **Ray Generation and Discretization**: The ray segment $[t_{start}, t_{end}]$ intersecting the volume is determined, typically by intersecting the ray with the volume's bounding box [S1, S8, S16, unofficial]. The segment is discretized into $N$ samples at equidistant intervals $\Delta t = (t_{end} - t_{start}) / N$ [S5, S10, S17, unofficial].
2.  **Sampling and Interpolation**: At each sample point $\mathbf{p}_i = r(t_i)$, the scalar value $d_i$ is retrieved from the volume data structure [S5, S10, unofficial]. This value is obtained by interpolating neighboring voxel values using a reconstruction kernel, most commonly trilinear interpolation of the eight surrounding voxels [S7, S10, S43, unofficial].
3.  **Classification (Transfer Function)**: The scalar value $d_i$ is mapped to optical properties: color $C_i$ and opacity $\alpha_i$ [S5, S10, S13, unofficial]. This mapping is performed by a transfer function $T(d_i) \rightarrow (C_i, \alpha_i)$ [S2, S2789]. The opacity is often corrected for the step size to account for the discretization error, using the relation $\alpha'_i = 1 - (1 - \alpha_i)^{\Delta t}$ or similar approximations [S11, S32, unofficial].
4.  **Compositing**: The optical properties are accumulated into the final pixel color using the [front-to-back volume rendering](#2350-front-to-back-volume-rendering.md) equation [S1, S13, unofficial][S56]. For each sample $i$ from front ($t_{start}$) to back ($t_{end}$), the accumulated color $C_{acc}$ and accumulated opacity $\alpha_{acc}$ are updated as follows:
    $$
    C_{acc}^{(i)} = C_{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha_{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alpha_i C_i
    $$
    $$
    \alpha_{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha_{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha_{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alpha_i
    $$
    where $C_{acc}^{(0)} = 0$ and $\alpha_{acc}^{(0)} = 0$ [S12, S43, unofficial][S50, abstract only, unofficial]. The term $(1 - \alpha_{acc}^{(i-1)})$ represents the transmittance, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample $i$ from the camera side [S1, S51, unofficial]. The final pixel color is often composited over a background color $C_{bg}$ using $C_{final} = C_{acc} + (1 - \alpha_{acc}) C_{bg}$ [S1, S14, unofficial].

Early ray termination is a common optimization where the loop breaks if $\alpha_{acc}$ exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1.0), as further samples contribute negligibly to the color [S10, S12, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Ray Marching and Discretization](2788-ray-marching-and-discretization.md)
An iterative [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) technique that approximates the [volume rendering integral](#8682-volume-rendering-integral.md) by casting rays from the camera through a 3D volume and accumulating optical properties at discrete sample points. It solves the problem of visualizing semi-transparent scalar fields without extracting explicit geometric surfaces by mapping data values to color and opacity via a transfer function and integrating the [emission-absorption model](#927-emission-absorption-model.md) along the viewing ray. Unlike fixed-step traversal methods, iterative variants advance rays using variable step sizes guided by distance estimators, enabling efficient handling of sparse, implicit, or procedural data. It processes the image pixel-by-pixel in a fragment shader, ensuring view-independent quality and supporting early ray termination.

### [Image-order Rendering Loop](2938-image-order-rendering-loop.md)
The fundamental control structure for [direct volume ray casting](#19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md), iterating over each pixel of the output image to generate a ray, traverse the volume, and composite the result. It solves the problem of mapping 3D volumetric data to a 2D image plane by decoupling the sampling process from the data structure, allowing for adaptive sampling and correct perspective projection in a single pass. Unlike object-order methods (rasterization), which process data primitives first, this approach is described as "CPU-like" but offers flexibility for advanced illumination and 32-bit compositing precision. It builds on the shared principles of [Image-order rendering](16-image-order-rendering.md) and [Ray Traversal and Integration Schemes](8341-ray-traversal-and-integration-schemes.md).

### [Front-to-Back Volume Ray Casting with HSV Shading and SOS/Attenuation/Reflection Filtering](4324-front-to-back-volume-ray-casting-with-hsv-shading-and-sos-at.md)
This method performs direct volume rendering by casting rays from the camera through each pixel into a 3D [volume, sampling](#7111-volume-sampling.md) voxel values along the ray path, and compositing them front-to-back to produce the final pixel color. It distinguishes itself from [standard ray casting](#3462-density-marching.md) by utilizing a multi-component volume value (Scalar Output Scalar, Attenuation, Reflection) to drive filtering and shading, converting these values to RGB via HSV color space, and applying specific attenuation-based opacity scaling. Unlike adaptive step methods, it typically employs a fixed number of steps with [early termination](#4675-early-termination.md) based on opacity saturation or volume boundaries.

### [LOS-integration for visualization](4807-los-integration-for-visualization.md)
[LOS-integration for visualization](#4807-los-integration-for-visualization.md) computes physical scalar quantities (electron column density, integrated emissivity, or emission-weighted temperature) along camera rays by integrating interpolated field values. It differs from standard direct volume rendering by outputting integrated physical metrics rather than a composited RGB image, reusing the ray sampling and field query infrastructure of the forward pass.

### [Monte Carlo Path Tracing for Volume Rendering](4980-monte-carlo-path-tracing-for-volume-rendering.md)
[Monte Carlo Path Tracing for Volume Rendering](#4980-monte-carlo-path-tracing-for-volume-rendering.md) (MCSRender) is a stochastic method for simulating light transport within participating media by sampling scattering events along rays rather than discretizing the path into fixed steps. Unlike deterministic [ray marching](#6739-ray-marching.md) which integrates the [volume rendering equation](#2098-volume-rendering-equation.md) via quadrature, this method uses [distance sampling](#8978-distance-sampling.md) to find [interaction](#41-interaction.md) points and accumulates results over multiple frames using an exponential moving average to converge to the solution. It is distinguished by its ability to handle complex scattering geometries and anisotropic lighting via environment maps without requiring a precomputed light field or voxelized light transport data.

### [Ray Traversal Schemes](6890-ray-traversal-schemes.md)
[Ray traversal schemes](#6890-ray-traversal-schemes.md) define how scalar voxel values are aggregated along a ray to produce a final pixel intensity, ranging from simple statistical projections to physically-based compositing. They solve the problem of mapping 3D volumetric data to 2D image space by determining which voxel properties (intensity, opacity, depth) contribute to the final pixel color. Unlike [Ray Marching and Discretization](2788-ray-marching-and-discretization.md), which focuses on the spatial sampling of the ray, these schemes focus on the mathematical aggregation function applied to the sampled values. They differ from [Monte Carlo Path Tracing for Volume Rendering](4980-monte-carlo-path-tracing-for-volume-rendering.md) by typically using deterministic, sequential accumulation rather than stochastic sampling.

### [Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting](9441-multi-layer-volume-ray-casting.md)
[Multi-layer volume ray casting](#9441-multi-layer-volume-ray-casting.md) is a unified rendering framework that handles complex volume-of-interest (VOI) interactions, including [clipping](#1444-clipping.md), [CSG operations](#1329-csg-operations-on-implicit-functions.md), embedded objects, and [empty-space skipping](#1002-empty-space-skipping.md), by encoding spatial overlaps into a pre-computed ray-layer buffer. Unlike standard single-layer [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) which processes a continuous ray or polygon-assisted methods that store full 3D coordinates, this method decomposes the ray into discrete, non-overlapping segments defined by material IDs and Z-coordinates, enabling segment-by-segment rendering with material-specific transfer functions in a single GPU pass. It sets itself apart by shifting the computational complexity of spatial intersection and priority resolution to a preprocessing depth-peeling stage, thereby keeping the per-pixel ray-casting loop simple and GPU-efficient.

### [Ray Casting and Compositing Loop](9826-ray-casting-and-compositing-loop.md)
This method defines the core computational loop for direct volume ray casting, responsible for sampling the volume, mapping data to optical properties, and accumulating color and opacity along a ray. It solves the problem of synthesizing a 2D image from a 3D scalar or vector field by evaluating the volume rendering equation. It is distinguished from [Ray Marching and Discretization](2788-ray-marching-and-discretization.md) by its explicit handling of the compositing accumulation and transfer function application within the integration step, and from [Monte Carlo Path Tracing for Volume Rendering](4980-monte-carlo-path-tracing-for-volume-rendering.md) by its deterministic, image-order approach.

### Spherical Volume Rendering with Adaptive Ray Casting
A method for expressing ocean scalar fields in a 3D digital Earth environment using a minimum bounding volume based on spherical mosaic as proxy geometry and adaptive sampling [S1, abstract only, unofficial]. It constructs a minimum bounding volume based on spherical mosaic as the proxy geometry, applies the depth texture of the seabed terrain to determine the position of sampling points in the spatial interpolation process, and proposes an adaptive sampling step algorithm based on heterogeneous depth distribution and data change rate to improve ray-casting efficiency [S1, abstract only, unofficial]. It also applies a nonlinear color-mapping enhancement scheme based on dataset skewness characteristics and designs a transparency transfer function to realize volume rendering and local feature structure extraction [S1, abstract only, unofficial].

## Background
The [shear-warp](#24-shear-warp.md) algorithm is used in the field of computer vision as a fast method of rendering the rotation of 3D volumes. It is based on the principle that, for a given perspective, the projection of a 3D volume when rotated about the centre is equal to the projection of the same volume after it has been sheared and then warped, which in the case of the shear-warp algorithm is a scaling along the vertical axis (Y axis in Fig. 2), see Fig. 3(b) [S1, abstract only, unofficial].
